candidates.label: Near Lions' Gate (St. Stephen's Gate), northeast corner of the Old City
candidates.support: The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places the Old Testament sheep gate (Nehemiah 3) "probably near the northeast corner" of Jerusalem's walls, and separately ties John 5:2's "sheep gate" to the nearby Pool of Bethesda. Today's Lions' Gate, also called St. Stephen's Gate, stands at that same northeast corner, close to the excavated pools identified with Bethesda, and is used here as the nearest confirmed point to this traditional area; no remains of an ancient sheep gate itself survive to fix an exact position.

summary.text: The sheep gate was one of the gates of Jerusalem's walls, rebuilt in Nehemiah's account of restoring the city, and probably stood near the wall's northeast corner. John's Gospel places a pool called Bethesda "by the sheep gate," where Jesus healed a man who had been sick for thirty-eight years.

history.text: The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek phrase translated "sheep gate" in John 5:2 could also be read as "sheep market," since the underlying word simply means something pertaining to sheep; either way, the reference ties the phrase to the nearby Pool of Bethesda rather than giving fresh topographical detail of its own.

scripture.textWEB: Now in Jerusalem by the sheep gate, there is a pool, which is called in Hebrew, “Bethesda”, having five porches.

otConnections.note: Nehemiah's account of rebuilding Jerusalem's walls after the exile has the priests build and consecrate the sheep gate, the earliest named occurrence of this gate.

politicalHistory.entity: Kingdom of Herod the Great (ruler: Herod the Great)
Ethnarchy of Judea, Samaria and Idumea (ruler: Herod Archelaus)
politicalHistory.note: The emperor Augustus did not grant Archelaus the royal title his father's will asked for, only "ethnarch." The first-century Jewish historian Josephus adds that Augustus took Gaza, Gadara and Hippos from Archelaus's share and added them to the province of Syria. The map doesn't draw Gaza's land separately, so it shows Gaza, and the coast south-west of it as far as Egypt, with this area.

politicalHistory.entity: Roman province of Judea (ruler: Prefects, e.g. Pontius Pilate)
politicalHistory.note: Luke links a census "when Quirinius was governor of Syria" to Jesus' birth, which Luke and Matthew place in Herod's days; the Jewish historian Josephus dates Quirinius's own census of Judea to this year. This map takes no position on how the accounts relate. The map shows Gaza and the coast south-west of it, as far as Egypt, with this area, since it doesn't draw them separately.
